record.original_question: Does there exist an optical fiber in R^3, in the sense of a reflective tube body with the almost-sure entrance and exit property described above, whose two planar ends are not congruent to each other?

evidence.quote: Suppose that V is a body in R^3 bounded by two plane figures F1 and F2 (the ends) and a smooth surface Σ (a tube). Suppose that a light ray entering V thru one end and bouncing with perfect reflection from the interior walls of Σ will emerge from the other end with probability 1; moreover, a light ray that emerges from the interior of V, after bouncing, emerges from one of the ends with probability 1. In this case, we say that V is an optical fiber.
In particular, Is there an optical fiber with noncongruent ends?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Call a body $V \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ an *optical fiber* if it satisfies the following conditions:

1. The boundary of $V$ consists of two planar regions $F_1$ and $F_2$ (the "ends"), together with a smooth surface $\Sigma$ (the "tube") meeting $F_1 \cup F_2$ along their boundary curves.
2. With probability $1$ (with respect to the natural measure on directions and entry points), a light ray entering the interior of $V$ through the relative interior of one end and undergoing perfectly specular reflection off $\Sigma$ at every encounter eventually exits through the other end.
3. With probability $1$, a light ray emitted from an interior point of $V$ in a uniformly random direction, after specular reflections off $\Sigma$, eventually exits through one of the two ends $F_1$ or $F_2$.

Question: Does there exist an optical fiber $V \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ whose two planar ends $F_1$ and $F_2$ are not congruent (i.e., not related by any rigid motion of the plane)?
